lead: Gas and liquid can meet in three flow arrangements. In co-current flow both enter at the same end and leave at the other. In counter-current flow gas rises while liquid falls. In cross-current flow gas passes stage after stage and fresh liquid enters each stage. The direction fixes the operating line, the average driving force and the best exit composition. Counter-current is the usual absorber; co-current suits fast washes; cross-current belongs mostly to leaching and extraction.
prereq: You need: the operating line and driving force from Chapter 3.2, and the pinch idea from Chapter 3.3.

blocks.text: Co-current. Gas and liquid enter together at one end. Write Y for kmol solute per kmol carrier gas and X for kmol solute per kmol solvent. L/G is the solvent-to-gas molar ratio, kmol solvent per kmol carrier gas. A solute balance from the inlet to any section gives G(Yin − Y) = L(X − Xin). Rearranged: Y = Yin − (L/G)(X − Xin). The operating line is straight with slope −L/G. It joins the mixed inlet point (Xin, Yin) to the mixed outlet point (Xout, Yout).

The equilibrium line is Y* = mX. Here m is the slope Y*/X: with Y and X as mole ratios, m is a dimensionless ratio, numerically kmol solvent per kmol carrier gas. At the outlet both streams leave the last stage together. With enough stages they approach equilibrium there, so Y<sub>out</sub> = mX<sub>out</sub>. Put this into the balance: G(Y<sub>in</sub> − mX<sub>out</sub>) = L(X<sub>out</sub> − X<sub>in</sub>). When X<sub>in</sub> = 0, X<sub>out</sub> = Y<sub>in</sub>/(m + L/G). More stages cannot push Y<sub>out</sub> below this value. Extra stages only bring the two outlet streams closer to that one equilibrium point.

sections.h3: Counter-current: opposite ends, largest driving force

blocks.text: Counter-current. Rich gas enters at the bottom. Lean liquid enters at the top. Gas flows up, liquid down. The operating line now runs from (Xout, Yin) at the bottom to (Xin, Yout) at the top. A balance from the top gives G(Y − Yout) = L(X − Xin), so Y = Yout + (L/G)(X − Xin). The slope is +L/G. The vertical gap Y − mX is the driving force. At the top, fresh liquid meets already-lean gas, so Yout can be small. At the bottom, partly loaded liquid meets rich gas, so the liquid can still take up solute. This opposite-end contact keeps a positive driving force over the whole column, as long as L/G is above the minimum (pinch) value from Chapter 3.3; below that value the operating line crosses the equilibrium line inside the column and the driving force turns negative somewhere. With L/G above the pinch, counter-current gives the largest average driving force of the three arrangements. That is why absorbers and strippers use counter-current flow. Packed height for this case is in Chapter 3.7.

Cross-current. Gas moves from stage to stage. Fresh liquid enters each stage and leaves that stage. Each stage has its own short solute balance, so the operating line is a set of short segments, not one long line. The first stage receives gas at Yin and leaves gas at Y1, with its liquid going from X0 to X1. Stage n receives gas at Yn−1 and leaves it at Yn, and its own fresh liquid goes from X0 to Xn. Every stage starts again from the same X0. Cross-current uses more liquid for the same removal. Each stage starts with fresh liquid, so its inlet driving force is larger than in counter-current at the same gas composition; over the whole cascade the average driving force is still smaller than counter-current's, which is why cross-current needs more solvent. In gas absorption it is rare because fresh solvent to every stage is costly. It is common in leaching and extraction; see Unit 5, Liquid Extraction and Leaching.

Choosing. For the same duty and the same solvent rate, counter-current needs the fewest stages and gives the leanest exit gas. Co-current gives the richest exit gas because its outlet is pinned by equilibrium, and it may fail to reach the duty no matter how many stages are added. Cross-current needs more stages than counter-current and more total solvent. Choose co-current for a fast irreversible wash, where the reaction removes the solute and equilibrium does not limit the outlet, and for heat-sensitive duties where a hot zone at one end must be avoided. Choose counter-current for normal absorption and stripping. Cross-current is chosen for leaching and extraction, not for a tall gas absorber.

figure.caption: Counter-current absorber with the worked example's compositions. Notice that the lean gas leaves at the top while the rich liquid leaves at the bottom.

examples.question: A gas stream enters an absorber with Y_in = 0.0526 kmol SO2/kmol air. The liquid enters with X_in = 0. The equilibrium line is Y* = 2X, with Y* in kmol SO2/kmol air and X in kmol SO2/kmol solvent. The liquid-to-gas ratio is L/G = 2.105 kmol solvent/kmol air. (a) In counter-current operation with Y_out = 0.00503, find X_out and check the bottom driving force. (b) In co-current operation at the same L/G, find the best possible X_out and Y_out. (c) Compare the exit gas compositions.
steps: Take a basis of G = 1 kmol air, so L = 2.105 kmol solvent.
Counter-current balance: G(Y_in − Y_out) = L(X_out − X_in). With X_in = 0, X_out = (Y_in − Y_out)/(L/G) = (0.0526 − 0.00503)/2.105 = 0.04757/2.105 = 0.0226 kmol SO2/kmol solvent.
Bottom driving force = Y_in − 2X_out = 0.0526 − 2(0.0226) = 0.0526 − 0.0452 = 0.0074 kmol SO2/kmol air. It is positive, so the operating line is feasible.

Co-current best outlet: both streams leave the last stage together, so Y_out = 2X_out. Balance: G(Y_in − Y_out) = L(X_out − 0). Substitute Y_out = 2X_out: 0.0526 − 2X_out = 2.105X_out. Thus 0.0526 = 4.105X_out and X_out = 0.0128 kmol SO2/kmol solvent.
Compare: 0.0256/0.00503 = 5.1. The co-current exit gas is about five times richer in SO2.
examples.answer: Counter-current: X_out = 0.0226 and Y_out = 0.00503. Co-current: X_out = 0.0128 and Y_out = 0.0256 kmol SO2/kmol solvent and air respectively; the counter-current exit gas is about 5.1 times leaner.
examples.check:
Yin = 0.0526
Yout_cc = 0.00503
LG = 2.105
m = 2
Xout_cc = (Yin - Yout_cc) / LG
Xout_co = Yin / (m + LG)
Yout_co = m * Xout_co
print(round(Yout_cc, 5))
print(round(Xout_cc, 4))
print(round(Xout_co, 4))
print(round(Yout_co, 4))

traps: More stages in a co-current absorber cannot give Y_out below the value set by equilibrium at the mixed outlet. The outlet is pinned by Y_out = mX_out.
Do not use slope −L/G for a counter-current absorber. On a Y–X plot the counter-current operating line slope is +L/G.
Cross-current is not the default for gas absorption. Fresh liquid to every stage is expensive; it is common in leaching and extraction.
In co-current flow both inlet streams enter at the same end. Do not draw the operating line from (X_in, Y_out) to (X_out, Y_in).

quiz.q: Name the three flow arrangements for gas and liquid in an absorber.
Why can a co-current absorber not reach any exit gas composition by adding stages?
quiz.a: The outlet gas and liquid leave the last stage together. With enough stages they approach equilibrium there, so Y_out = mX_out. More stages cannot cross that limit.

quiz.q: Use the worked example's equilibrium line and Y_in = 0.0526. For co-current flow with L/G = 4.0 and X_in = 0, find the best X_out and Y_out.
quiz.a: X_out = Y_in/(m + L/G) = 0.0526/(2 + 4.0) = 0.00877 kmol SO2/kmol solvent. Y_out = 2X_out = 0.0175 kmol SO2/kmol air.

quiz.q: For the same duty and L/G, why does counter-current need fewer stages than co-current?
quiz.a: Counter-current keeps a positive driving force along the whole column, so the average driving force is large. In co-current the driving force falls to zero at the outlet because the two outlet streams approach equilibrium there.

quiz.q: In a counter-current absorber, at which ends do lean gas and rich liquid leave?
quiz.a: Lean gas leaves at the top. Rich liquid leaves at the bottom.

quiz.q: What shape does a cross-current operating line have, and why?
quiz.a: It is a set of short segments. Fresh liquid enters each stage, so each stage starts a new solute balance from the same X_0.

quiz.q: In the counter-current example, compute the top driving force Y_out − 2X_in.
quiz.a: Y_out − 2X_in = 0.00503 − 2(0) = 0.00503 kmol SO2/kmol air. It is positive.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industrial absorbers are built counter-current because solvent regeneration is the main operating cost. Co-current contact appears in venturi scrubbers and fast reactive washes where the reaction, not equilibrium, controls the outlet. Cross-current staging is standard in leaching and extraction, as Unit 5 shows. Rotating packed beds and membrane contactors are newer designs, but flow direction still sets the local driving force. Search 'co-current absorption', 'cross-current leaching' and 'rotating packed bed absorption'.
